name: INTEGRATED LAND USE PLANNING AND SUSTAINABLE LAND USE SYSTEMS FOR LDN
description: This level encompasses the operational frameworks and analytical processes required to guide land users in achieving Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) through science-based and participatory decision-making. It combines integrated land use planning ILUP, sustainable land management SLM and sustainable land use systems SLUS. ILUP provides a systematic, cross-sectoral and multi-stakeholder framework for deciding where and for what land is used. SLM provides the practices that avoid, reduce and reverse land and soil degradation on agricultural lands in line with the LDN response hierarchy. SLUS add a broader social–ecological systems perspective to the configuration and governance of land-use mosaics, value chains and institutions across landscapes. Building on robust biophysical and socioeconomic assessments, these approaches together enable the identification of degradation hotspots, the anticipation of land-use trends, the management of trade-offs among competing land uses and the spatial targeting of context-specific SLM practices to balance anticipated losses with planned gains. Monitoring systems track global LDN indicators—land cover, productivity and soil organic carbon—alongside locally relevant metrics to validate progress, support adaptive management and ensure social and environmental safeguards.

name: INTEGRATED, DIVERSIFIED AND RESILIENT PRODUCTION SYSTEMS
description: This level focuses on the operationalization of long-term integrated strategies through on-the-ground land-interventions that rehabilitate, conserve, and sustainably manage land and water resources. By applying locally led, context specific, and holistic approaches, it seeks to actively avoid, reduce, and reverse the degradation of agricultural lands and soils. The overarching objective is to transition toward sustainable, socioeconomically viable, and resilient agrifood systems grounded in healthy and fertile soils. Implementation draws on Ecosystem-based solutions and ecosystem-based approaches to establish biodiversity-friendly cropping systems. The three clusters - Cropland, Grazing land, and Supporting Ecosystems - should be addressed in an integrated way in order to maximize synergies across activities and ensure coherent, landscape-level outcomes.

name: ENABLING ENVIRONMENT
description: The Enabling Environment for Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) encompasses the interlinked institutional, policy-regulatory, financial, market, capacity, and science–policy conditions that collectively enable countries to avoid, reduce, and reverse land degradation in a sustained and socially equitable manner. At its core, the enabling environment relies on Policy coherence, ensuring that land, soil, water, food, energy, climate, biodiversity, and development policies are aligned, mutually supportive, and free from contradictory incentives. Effective Integrated governance of soil, land and water provides the institutional and legal foundation for LDN implementation. The enabling environment is further strengthened through Resource mobilization and investment, which aligns national budgets, public expenditures, and financial regulations with LDN targets. Well-functioning Markets play a complementary role by shaping incentives for land users and economic actors. Cross-cutting Institutional capacity development underpins all clusters by strengthening the human, organizational, and systemic capacities required to design, coordinate, implement, and sustain LDN actions. Finally, Science and innovation connect evidence to action through robust science–policy interfaces, monitoring systems, digital platforms, and participatory knowledge processes.

name: Assessment
description: This cluster provides the evidence base required to support ILUP, SLM and SLUS in pursuit of LDN. It characterizes the state and severity of land degradation to inform actions that avoid, reduce and reverse degradation. By systematically assessing natural resources—including soil, land and water resources—and land potential, it underpins spatial planning decisions on land use, the selection and targeting of SLM practices and analysis of how different land-use configurations perform as sustainable land use systems. It also includes gender-sensitive socioeconomic analysis to understand livelihoods, access to resources and differential vulnerability, and integrates biophysical and socioeconomic data to map land uses, land users and stakeholders, including through the use of early warning systems.

name: Planning
description: This cluster supports the implementation of LDN by helping countries move from planning to practice. It draws on integrated land use planning ILUP, sustainable land management SLM and sustainable land use systems SLUS to translate assessments and stakeholder priorities into spatially explicit, actionable pathways for LDN. Building on ILUP guidance, it establishes a shared vision and identifies priority areas by applying the LDN response hierarchy to avoid, reduce and reverse degradation and by explicitly considering where different land uses and SLM practices are best placed. Drawing on SLUS concepts, it considers how these spatial decisions, management choices, value chains and institutions interact to shape social, environmental and economic outcomes across the landscape. Spatial analysis is used to link land-use decisions with context-specific SLM options, optimize resource use, manage trade-offs among competing land uses and counterbalance anticipated losses with planned gains. Finally, this cluster supports the preparation of roadmaps, implementation plans and programme portfolios that align ILUP, SLM and SLUS to restore, conserve and use land and water resources sustainably.

name: Monitoring and adapting
description: The Monitoring cluster focuses on establishing robust systems to track progress towards land degradation neutrality by measuring trends in land cover, land productivity, and carbon stocks against a fixed baseline to determine net gains and losses. It assesses the performance of sustainable land management and ecosystem restoration by tracking soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks and soil health to verify the effectiveness of interventions. Moving beyond single-crop yields, this cluster evaluates sustainable productivity through Total Factor Productivity (TFP) and resource use efficiency to ensure production does not compromise natural resources or ecosystem services. Crucially, it implements comprehensive assessment frameworks to monitor socio-economic impacts, with a specific focus on food security, gender equality, and the resilience of vulnerable communities to shocks and stresses. It also involves participatory monitoring of responsible governance to assess tenure security and the recognition of legitimate rights, particularly for Indigenous Peoples, and other groups, including local communities. Finally, it utilizes early warning systems to conduct continuous vulnerability and risk assessments, tracking hazard exposure and water scarcity to anticipate impacts before they escalate.

name: Cropland
description: This cluster focuses on implementing diversification strategies to establish drought-resistant cropping systems that support land and soil restoration. The application of Sustainable Land Management (SLM) and Sustainable Soil Management (SSM) harnesses natural processes, promotes beneficial biological interactions and synergies, enhances ecosystem services, and contributes to more diverse, resilient, and productive cropping systems. Increasing crop diversity - including neglected and underutilized species - can improve dietary diversity and nutrition, while also enhancing climate resilience and soil health. The result is more diverse, resilient, and productive cropping systems that contribute to long-term sustainability and improved soil functionality.

name: Grazing land
description: This cluster addresses the management of pastures and livestock to prevent land degradation and enhance ecological functions. It includes a toolkit with voluntary measures, that, among others, could formally support pastoral mobility and indigenous peoples, recognizing and protecting the collective and customary rights that underpin traditional, flexible grazing land management, according to national legislation. It also covers sustainable grazing land management approaches, such as managing grazing pressure (for example, through rotational grazing or rangeland resting), to promote productivity, prevent degradation, and support soil carbon storage.

name: Supporting Ecosystems
description: This cluster focuses on the application of ecosystem-based approaches to sustain land productivity, restore degraded ecosystems, and enhance the resilience of agrifood systems to climate change. These approaches harness ecological processes and biodiversity to deliver multiple co-benefits - supporting climate adaptation and mitigation, improving water and soil health, and strengthening livelihoods. Ecosystem-based solutions in this context include a range of interventions such as agroforestry, integrated watershed and landscape management, and the conservation or restoration of natural habitats within agricultural areas. These practices contribute to the creation of multifunctional landscapes that maintain ecological integrity, enhance ecosystem services, and reduce vulnerability to environmental shocks. By embedding these strategies within broader land-use planning and community-led governance, this cluster reinforces the SLUS principles of systems thinking, participatory decision-making, and integration across land uses. Ecosystem-based solutions are particularly effective when implemented alongside sustainable cropping and grazing systems, as they provide the ecological foundation - healthy soils, water regulation, biodiversity corridors - upon which productive and resilient agrifood systems depend.

name: Policy coherence
description: The Policy coherence cluster focuses on establishing long-term strategies for the restoration, conservation and sustainable management of land and water resources to minimize and reverse desertification and land degradation. It entails the systematic alignment of legal frameworks with governance of soil, land and water standards, specifically the Voluntary Guidelines for the Responsible Governance of Tenure (VGGT), to ensure tenure security is not compromised. To minimize trade-offs and maximize synergies, this cluster promotes integrated resources management and the coordination of sustainable land and soil management across sectors to address additional stresses on land. It further advances inclusive governance that integrates local and traditional practices and locally led, contextually relevant, and holistic approaches into decision-making to support biodiversity, drought resilience and food security. In addition, the cluster encourages the strategic alignment of public policies and investments in food and agriculture to ensure that sustainable land use and management are pursued alongside broader social, economic, and environmental objectives, thereby strengthening overall policy coherence across development priorities.

name: Markets and value chains
description: The Markets and value chains cluster supports the transition toward sustainable, socioeconomically viable, and resilient agriculture and food systems by strengthening the economic agency of farmers, including smallholders, and Indigenous Peoples' food generation schemes. It promotes inclusive market systems through enabling policy frameworks and partnerships that reinforce rural–urban linkages, support producer organizations, and expand equitable market access. Anchored in the Sustainable Food Value Chain framework developed by FAO and UNIDO, the cluster adopts a systems-based approach that considers the full range of actors—from production to consumption—and the broader institutional, economic, social, and environmental context in which value chains operate. In line with this framework, value-chain interventions are guided by the integration of three interdependent dimensions of sustainability: economic viability, ensuring value creation and fair distribution of benefits; social inclusion, promoting equitable participation, decent work, and improved nutrition; and environmental stewardship, minimizing negative impacts on ecosystems, biodiversity, water, and soil while enhancing resilience to shocks and stresses. To contribute to food security and the reliable supply of nutritious, locally adapted, and diverse crops, the cluster prioritizes strategic investments in enabling infrastructure—such as storage facilities, logistics systems, and cold chains—to reduce post-harvest losses, improve market functioning, and strengthen the resilience of livelihoods dependent on agrifood systems.

name: Integrated Governance of soil, land and water
description: This cluster focuses on strengthening integrated governance frameworks that guide the sustainable management of land, soil and water resources. It promotes coherent policy frameworks, inclusive governance structures and transparent institutional arrangements that enable coordinated decision-making across sectors such as agriculture, environment and land-use planning. Guided by internationally recognized frameworks, including the Voluntary Guidelines on the Responsible Governance of Tenure of Land, Fisheries and Forests, the World Soil Charter and the Voluntary Guidelines for Sustainable Soil Management, the cluster promotes responsible governance systems that ensure equitable access to land and water resources while safeguarding soil health. It can support the development of inclusive policies, multi-level governance mechanisms and participatory decision-making processes involving governments, civil society, Indigenous Peoples, as well as other groups including local communities, in accordance with national circumstances and legislation. Particular attention may be given, as appropriate, to securing legitimate tenure rights, strengthening gender-responsive land governance and addressing risks of dispossession and exclusion affecting vulnerable groups.

name: Resource mobilization and investment
description: The Resource mobilization and investment cluster focuses on establishing the financial enabling environment required to implement long-term integrated strategies for sustainable land management. It emphasizes the need to invest in the development of innovative science-based sustainable solutions and partnerships between public, private, and financial sectors to mobilize capital. To ensure national budgets align with these objectives, this cluster prioritizes conducting financial needs assessments and analyzing public expenditures to redirect subsidies that may be harmful to biodiversity or land health toward investments that yield long-term benefits. It seeks to create a stable and transparent regulatory environment that incentivizes responsible private investment in sustainable agriculture and land restoration while managing risks. Finally, it promotes the use of blended finance mechanisms and de-risking strategies to support investments in Ecosystem-based solutions and ecosystem-based approaches, thereby enhancing productivity and resilience.

name: Science and innovation
description: The Science and Innovation Cluster focuses on the systematic generation, validation, documentation, and sharing of knowledge to support sustainable, resilient, and climate-adapted agrifood systems. It strengthens the links between scientific research, policy processes, and local knowledge systems, ensuring that decisions related to land, soil, water, and ecosystem management are evidence-based, inclusive, and responsive to changing environmental conditions. This cluster promotes the integration of scientific evidence, geospatial data, digital tools, and experiential knowledge from farmers, pastoralists, and Indigenous Peoples to guide sustainable land management and ecosystem restoration. By fostering science–policy interfaces, participatory learning approaches, and knowledge-sharing platforms, it enables stakeholders at multiple scales—from local land users to national policymakers—to access reliable information, co-develop solutions, and scale up effective practices. In doing so, it recognizes the specific collective rights of Indigenous Peoples (including data sovereignty, FPIC and knowledge ownership) as foundational principles guiding the generation and use of knowledge. Through strengthened monitoring systems, digital innovation, and institutional capacity development, the cluster supports transparent reporting, adaptive management, and the implementation of global commitments related to land degradation neutrality, climate change adaptation, biodiversity conservation, and ecosystem restoration.

name: Characterize Land Degradation of Agricultural Land
description: Assess the state, extent, and severity of land degradation by identifying physical, chemical, and biological deterioration processes - such as soil erosion, salinization, and loss of biodiversity - to determine the reduction in the land's capacity to provide ecosystem services over time and under climate change and drought pressures, and to identify desertification sensitivity and ecosystem vulnerability.
Related activities: Monitor LDN Achievement|Define Priority Areas of Intervention

name: Characterize Land and Soil Resources and Uses
description: Conduct a systematic inventory of land-based natural resources by analyzing soil properties, biodiversity (e.g., ecological connectivity, habitat quality, species richness), topography, and vegetative cover to establish a comprehensive spatial database for Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) planning. Classify land units and land types based on inherent land potential—determined by soil texture, depth, mineralogy, and thermal climates—to ensure a scientific basis for matching land-use requirements with biophysical limitations.

name: Characterize Water Resources
description: Conduct a comprehensive assessment of water resources by analyzing precipitation, evapotranspiration, and hydrological regimes at the watershed or basin level. Implement water accounting and auditing to systematically document stocks, flows, and fluxes to underpin Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM). Characterize water stress, water scarcity, and historical drought frequency across different production systems.
Related activities: Monitor LDN Achievement

name: Characterize Land and Soil Management
description: Assess current land use practices - including agronomic, vegetative, structural, and management measures - to determine their impact on resource sustainability and productivity. This involves documenting existing approaches, such as conservation agriculture, agroforestry, or grazing management, and evaluating their effectiveness in maintaining ecosystem functions, controlling degradation, and supporting livelihoods.
Related activities: Monitor Sustainable Land and Soil Management Performance

name: Characterize Land Productivity, Suitability and Potential
description: Evaluate the capacity of land resources to support specific land utilization types by matching crop and livestock requirements with agro-climatic and edaphic conditions to determine attainable yields and production gaps. This process involves using land evaluation protocols to classify land suitability - from prime to unsuitable - under different management scenarios, thereby identifying opportunities to optimize resource use efficiency without compromising ecosystem functions. Where relevant, this assessment should also consider alternative land-based uses, including non-food biomass and bioenergy feedstocks, to identify potential synergies and trade-offs with food production, soil health, water resources and land degradation outcomes. Crucially, integrate projected climate impacts and future land-use scenarios by utilizing advanced tools like GAEZ v5 and Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) to anticipate geographic shifts in land suitability and desertification sensitivity and to inform forward-looking decisions under changing climatic and socio-economic conditions.
Related activities: Monitor Sustainable Productivity

name: Analyze Socio-Economic Context, Gender, and Vulnerability of farmers, Indigenous Peoples and pastoralists
description: Conduct a comprehensive gender-sensitive analysis of the socioeconomic environment by examining livelihood strategies, access to productive resources, and tenure security to understand how structural inequalities shape the differential vulnerability of men, women, and youth to shocks and stresses. This entails examining power dynamics and resource control to ensure that interventions address the specific constraints faced by vulnerable groups and strengthen their adaptive capacity against climate and economic instability. Include the nutritional dimensions of vulnerability, including household dietary diversity, food security, access to and affordability of nutritious foods, and dependence on subsistence production for dietary needs.
Related activities: Monitor Social Impacts and Equity

name: Characterize Land Uses and Stakeholders
description: Map and describe current land use systems and the associated actors by integrating biophysical land cover data with socioeconomic attributes to understand human-environment interactions and conflicting interests regarding resource management. This involves identifying all direct and indirect stakeholders and analyzing their rights, responsibilities, and power relations through participatory methods (e.g., community mapping, traditional management practices) to ensure that planning processes are inclusive and reflect the diverse needs and aspirations of those managing the land.

name: Conduct Integrated Causal Analysis of Land Degradation Drivers
description: Utilize the Driver–Pressure–State–Impact–Response (DPSIR) framework to identify eventual causal links between human activities when existing (e.g., unsustainable management practices, population growth, land tenure insecurity) and the deteriorating state of land, soil, and water resources. Utilize Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to overlay spatial trends in global indicators—such as Soil Organic Carbon (SOC), Net Primary Productivity (NPP), and Land Cover Change (LCC)—with socio-economic variables like poverty levels, access rights, and market infrastructure.
Related activities: Define Priority Areas of Intervention|Ensure Cross-Sectoral Policy Coherence with Competing Uses

name: Assess Vulnerability and Resilience
description: Conduct comprehensive vulnerability and resilience assessments to identify at-risk populations and ecosystems that are most susceptible to harm. This involves analyzing the unique combination of exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity within the specific socio-ecological system to determine where interventions will be most effective, particularly in areas vulnerable to desertification and climate-induced land degradation.
Related activities: Monitor Vulnerability and Resilience

name: Set Up Early Warning Systems
description: Establish and operationalize multi-hazard monitoring and early warning systems that integrate meteorological, agricultural, and livelihood data to detect emerging threats—such as drought, pests, and climate variability—before they escalate into crises.
Related activities: Monitor Early Warning Systems

name: Define Vision and Objectives for the Landscape(s)
description: Develop a long-term, shared vision for the target landscape(s) based on validated information from the LDN targets assessment and aligned with (LDN) principles and national targets.
Related activities: Characterize Land Degradation of Agricultural Land |Ensure Cross-Sectoral Policy Coherence with Competing Uses

name: Define Priority Areas of Intervention
description: Locate areas where land degradation is most urgent and where interventions will be most effective. It involves mapping current and potential degradation, validating existing hotspots through stakeholder workshops, and reviewing datasets, land-use contexts, drivers of degradation, while also taking into account areas affected by conflicts. Anticipate future degradation, identify priority areas for sustainable land management interventions, and ensure alignment with the shared LDN vision and validated assessment data.
Related activities: Characterize Land Degradation of Agricultural Land |Characterize Land Uses and Stakeholders |Conduct Integrated Causal Analysis of Land Degradation Drivers

name: Identify and Prioritize SLM Practices
description: Compile a context-specific set of SLM practices that integrates scientific evidence with indigenous and traditional knowledge systems with demonstrated potential to address identified degradation, causes and their drivers. Assess their effects on key ecosystem services and carbon sequestration and their short- and long-term costs and benefits, while validating the effectiveness of local and customary approaches. Identify any additional suitable practices and prioritise all relevant options through a participatory process that fosters the co-creation of knowledge to address priority areas and underlying LD drivers. In doing so, apply the Principles for Locally Led Adaptation (LLA) to ensure communities hold genuine decision-making authority — not merely a consultative role — over the selection and prioritization of practices.
Related activities: Characterize Land and Soil Management |Analyze Socio-Economic Context, Gender, and Vulnerability of farmers, Indigenous Peoples and pastoralists |Include Traditional Knowledge in Planning

name: Design and Spatially Prioritize SLM Interventions
description: Link SLM practices to Priority Areas, evaluate their feasibility, and determine where and when they should be implemented. The activity includes preparing a matrix of suitable practices with priority areas, selecting and analysing top-prioritised options, assessing their costs for project-level implementation, and allocating them spatially using GIS. It also identifies lower-priority areas where practices can be phased in later or used as counterbalancing options. The spatial prioritisation process should incorporate carbon storage potential as an additional layer in GIS-based analysis, ensuring that vegetation-based interventions are allocated to areas that combine high degradation severity with high carbon sequestration opportunity.
Related activities: Characterize Land Productivity, Suitability and Potential

name: Develop an Implementation Roadmap
description: Develop a detailed implementation roadmap that specifies roles, responsibilities, locations, timelines, and modalities for carrying out the selected interventions. Validate this roadmap through a multi-stakeholder workshop to review and confirm roles, responsibilities, and timelines, and to identify potential barriers and corresponding solutions using the Landscape Matrix.
Related activities: Conduct Financial Needs Assessments and Budget Alignment

name: Monitor LDN Achievement
description: Establish and implement robust monitoring systems that track Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) status by measuring trends in land cover, land productivity, and soil carbon stocks against a fixed baseline to determine net gains and losses and the land area affected (LAA). To ensure accuracy, global datasets should be validated with national data, field assessments, and participatory inputs from local stakeholders to confirm that observed changes accurately reflect ground conditions.
Related activities: Characterize Land Degradation of Agricultural Land |Characterize Water Resources

name: Monitor Sustainable Land and Soil Management Performance
description: Assess and track the performance of sustainable land management practices by measuring soil organic carbon stocks, soil health and biodiversity, and land productivity dynamics to verify the effectiveness of interventions. This involves utilizing standardized protocols and integrating scientific data with local knowledge to evaluate improvements in biomass production, nutrient cycling, and water use efficiency, ensuring that agricultural intensification remains sustainable. Monitoring of SLM performance should include the assessment of carbon sequestration outcomes, capturing both soil organic carbon stocks and above- and below-ground biomass carbon, to evaluate the contribution of land management practices to climate mitigation.
Related activities: Characterize Land and Soil Management |Promote Sustainable Land Management and Cropping Diversity |Promote Sustainable Grazing and Land Management

name: Monitor Sustainable Productivity
description: Assess the long-term viability of agricultural systems by measuring Total Factor Productivity (TFP) and resource use efficiency - rather than solely relying on single-crop yields - to ensure that production gains do not compromise natural resources or ecosystem services. This approach extends traditional accounting to explicitly include non-marketed environmental goods and services, such as soil health and water availability, while also accounting for negative externalities like pollution.
Related activities: Characterize Land Productivity, Suitability and Potential

name: Monitor Social Impacts and Equity
description: Implement comprehensive assessment frameworks to monitor the socio-economic impacts of land use changes, focusing on food security, nutrition, gender equality, and the resilience of vulnerable communities to climate shocks. This involves using resilience diagnostic tools and disaggregated data to evaluate the capacity of households to absorb and recover from stresses, ensuring that land-based interventions support livelihoods and do not exacerbate existing inequalities.
Related activities: Analyze Socio-Economic Context, Gender, and Vulnerability of farmers, Indigenous Peoples and pastoralists

name: Monitor Governance of Tenure
description: Develop and apply participatory monitoring frameworks to assess the security of tenure and the recognition of legitimate rights, particularly for Indigenous Peoples, as well as other groups such as local communities, according to national legislation. This involves using tools such as participatory mapping and community-led registries to document resource access, track the implementation of legal reforms, and identify emerging conflicts over natural resources to prevent dispossession and ensure equitable governance.
Related activities: Legally Recognize and Respect All Legitimate Tenure Rights

name: Monitor Vulnerability and Resilience
description: Establish a dynamic monitoring system to track the progress of resilience-building activities and assess the evolving capacity of your agrifood system to absorb, recover from, and transform in the face of shocks.
Related activities: Assess Vulnerability and Resilience

name: Monitor Early Warning Systems
description: Establish a continuous monitoring framework that functions as a repository for climate data, drought indicators, and socio-economic variables to detect 'weak signals' of emerging threats before they escalate into crises.
Related activities: Set Up Early Warning Systems

name: Institutional capacity development
description: This cross-cutting cluster strengthens the human, organizational, and systemic capacities essential for implementing LDN and sustaining its outcomes. It focuses on empowering people and institutions at all levels — from local land users and extension agents to national ministries and inter-institutional bodies — so that the guidance's technical and policy measures can be effectively carried out and maintained over time. Unlike other clusters that address what to do (e.g. specific land management practices, policies, or monitoring tools), this cluster addresses how to build an enabling environment of skilled stakeholders, capable institutions, and collaborative networks. It promotes a culture of learning, partnership, and innovation, ensuring that interventions are locally owned and adaptive. Consistent with FAO's capacity development approach, it targets three interrelated levels — individuals (knowledge and skills), organizations (structures, mandates, and resources), and the enabling environment (policies, incentives, and partnerships). By assessing capacity gaps and systematically addressing them through training, knowledge-sharing platforms, institutional strengthening, and the inclusion of under-represented groups (youth, women, Indigenous Peoples), countries can enhance their ability to plan, coordinate, and scale up LDN interventions.

description: Implement sustainable land management practices and approaches, including measures such as minimum soil disturbance, crop rotation, cover crops, crop diversification, and agroforestry, where appropriate, to support soil health, improve water infiltration, reduce erosion, and contribute to sustainable agricultural production systems, including through diversified agricultural and regenerative approaches that may contribute to soil carbon enhancement, biodiversity conservation, and greenhouse gas mitigation co-benefits.

name: Integrate Cropping Systems with Grazing/Livestock Systems
description: Integrated Crop-Livestock Systems (ICLS), or agropastoral systems, involve the integration of crop and livestock enterprises to promote biological interactions between the two activities. These systems may include the use of animal manure to fertilize crops, contributing to nutrient recycling and potentially reducing the use of external inputs. Their implementation within climate-smart agriculture approaches may vary according to national contexts, regulatory frameworks, and production systems.
Related activities: Integrate Livestock Systems with Cropping Systems

name: Manage Salinity, Sodicity, Waterlogging and Drainage
description: Diagnose and address soil salinity, sodicity, waterlogging and inadequate drainage in irrigated and rain-fed agricultural lands through an integrated set of measures: drainage infrastructure rehabilitation, controlled leaching, gypsum amendments for sodic soils, irrigation water quality management, salt-tolerant varieties, and water table monitoring. Programme design should be grounded in baseline soil and hydrological assessment (EC, ESP, water table depth) and embedded within irrigation district or watershed management plans, with progress tracked through national LDN monitoring frameworks.

name: Support Pastoral Mobility
description: Develop and implement development strategies, legal frameworks, and agreements that secure pastoral mobility and transhumance, including transboundary passage, to allow rotational use of wet- and dry-season grazing areas. This includes mobile pastoralism and transhumance corridor mapping guidance, with specific activities on mapping stock routes, dry-season grazing reserves, and water points to reduce conflict and prevent localized overgrazing. It also involves recognizing and protecting customary tenure rights and managing stock routes and water points to prevent overgrazing and land degradation caused by the restriction of movement.

name: Promote Sustainable Grazing and Land Management
description: Employ strategies to manipulate the soil-plant-animal complex to maintain or restore vegetation cover, soil health, and ecosystem services. Key practices include grazing pressure management through techniques such as rotational grazing (shifting livestock between paddocks or areas), mobility, and rangeland resting (deferment or enclosures) to allow forage recovery and prevent overgrazing. Sustainable grazing practices should be implemented to preserve vegetation cover, reduce soil degradation, and protect vulnerable landscapes. Integrate livestock early warning and drought monitoring systems, including the use of climate, vegetation, and drought data to support timely decision-making by herders and livestock managers.

name: Improve Animal Health and Welfare
description: Strengthen surveillance and response systems for diseases emerging from livestock production and reduce the risk of zoonoses. Related activities: Promote Sustainable Land Management and Cropping Diversity

name: Manage and Conserve Animal Genetic Resources
description: Promote the use and conservation of locally adapted breeds that are hardy, disease-resistant, and able to cope with harsh environmental conditions (e.g., heat stress, drought). name: Integrate Livestock Systems with Cropping Systems
description: Implement Agropastoralism or Integrated Crop-Livestock Systems (ICLS) to diversify production and foster biological synergies. This involves grazing livestock on crop residues, stubble, and fallow lands to provide supplemental feed, particularly during dry seasons or droughts when pasture is scarce. It includes a toolkit with voluntary measures that, among others, could support integrated and mobile livestock management practices, according to national legislation.

name: Implement Agroforestry Systems
description: Integrate trees with crops and/or livestock on the same land management unit to provide shade, drive soil improvement, and generate additional yields. Recognized as a vital agroecological and ecosystem-based adaptation practice, it enhances soil health and water retention, thereby increasing resilience to climate change and helping to combat desertification, land degradation and drought. By diversifying production, it supports food security and contributes to both climate change adaptation and mitigation.

name: Implement Integrated Landscape and Watershed Management

name: Restore Riparian Buffers and Permanent Protection Areas
description: Restore and maintain vegetated buffer zones along watercourses, wetlands and other sensitive areas to reduce diffuse agricultural pollution, regulate water flows and provide biodiversity corridors within agricultural landscapes. By re-establishing permanent vegetation cover in riparian zones and legally designated protection areas, this activity enhances soil conservation, improves water quality and strengthens ecological connectivity in support of LDN reverse interventions and integrated watershed management.

The sustainable management, conservation, and restoration of ecosystems - such as wetlands, forests, and agroecosystems - maintains and increases resilience while reducing the vulnerability of both ecosystems and communities to climate hazards. Secure the delivery of essential provisioning and regulating services, such as water regulation and soil protection, to buffer against extreme events like floods and droughts.
